sections.heading: Thanking you for making me able to know you
sections.text: Creator and Redeemer, I worship you because everything I am and everything I have begins with you. You made me more than a body moving through the world. You gave me a mind that can seek truth, a conscience that can feel the weight of right and wrong, and a heart that can be stirred to want you. Even my desire for you is your mercy at work in me.
theological_themes: human dignity as creatures made able to know God
conscience and spiritual desire as gifts of grace

scripture_references.connection: Paul presents God as the maker and sustainer of all people, the one in whom we live and move and have our being. This supports the prayer’s gratitude that existence, rational life, and the possibility of seeking God all come from him.

Paul describes conscience as part of the moral awareness God has placed in human beings. That gives biblical grounding to thanking God for conscience without treating conscience as sufficient for salvation.

sections.heading: Praising you for showing your mercy in the gospel
sections.text: Thank you for not leaving me to guess what you are like. In the gospel you have opened your heart to sinners. You have shown me that you are full of compassion, that your purposes toward me in Christ are peace and not destruction, and that your patience is wider than I can measure. Your mercy is not small or reluctant; it is deep enough for people like me.
theological_themes: God reveals himself in the gospel
divine mercy and patience toward sinners

scripture_references.connection: Paul says God gives the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ. This grounds the prayer’s praise that God has revealed himself truly and savingly in the gospel.

This passage connects justification by faith with peace with God through Jesus Christ. It supports the prayer’s confidence that God’s intentions toward the believer are peace because of Christ, not because of personal worthiness.
Paul points to his own salvation as a display of Christ’s perfect patience toward sinners. That fits the prayer’s praise for God’s patience and generous mercy.

sections.heading: Asking to know salvation as something real now
sections.text: You have awakened my conscience to the questions I cannot answer on my own: How can my guilt be forgiven? How can an unclean heart be made holy? How can someone spiritually poor become rich before you? Keep me from being content with hearing true things from a distance. Let me truly know you, walk with you, enjoy you, trust what you have said, and find life in your word.

scripture_references.connection: God promises cleansing, a new heart, and his Spirit within his people. This speaks directly to the prayer’s longing for pardon and real inward renewal, not mere religious appearance.
Paul ties redemption and forgiveness to the riches of God’s grace in Christ. This supports the prayer’s language of the guilty being pardoned and the spiritually poor being enriched.
James warns against merely hearing the word without doing it. This grounds the prayer’s desire to be among those who not only hear about God but live in responsive trust and obedience.

sections.heading: Longing for the Spirit’s present help
sections.text: Father, I do not want salvation to be only a doctrine I can explain. I want to taste its comfort and strength today by your Holy Spirit. Give me the graces that make a life beautiful to you. Teach me to value not only the gifts and privileges you give me, but also the ordinary responsibilities you put in front of me. Make my faith simple, honest, and sincere.
theological_themes: present experience of salvation by the Holy Spirit
spiritual graces expressed in ordinary obedience

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the Spirit’s work in giving believers the cry of adoption and bearing witness that they are God’s children. This supports the prayer’s longing for present comfort and rejoicing in salvation.
The fruit of the Spirit names the graces God produces in his people. This fits the prayer’s request for spiritual blessings that take visible shape in character.
Paul speaks of living with simplicity and godly sincerity by the grace of God. That directly illuminates the prayer’s desire for an honest, uncomplicated life before God.

sections.heading: Making my life true before you and useful to others
sections.text: Please make me the same person before you that I appear to be before other people. Let my heart belong to you before my mouth claims that it does. Keep me from carrying the world’s loves into a religious life and pretending nothing is wrong. Turn my desires toward what is above. Help me avoid empty pleasures and forbidden compromises. And do not let me only receive grace—make me someone who shares it. Prepare me both to do good and to endure hardship faithfully when it comes.
theological_themes: setting the heart on heavenly things
faithfulness in doing good and bearing suffering

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls believers raised with Christ to seek the things above and put earthly, sinful desires to death. This supports the prayer’s plea for affections directed toward God rather than forbidden or empty things.
Peter teaches that those who have received grace are to steward it in serving others. This fits the prayer’s request to be a dispenser of grace, not only a recipient.
Peter connects patient endurance under unjust suffering with following Christ’s example. This grounds the prayer’s desire to be ready not only to do good but also to bear evil faithfully.

sections.heading: Wanting Jesus to be honored in me
sections.text: God, make me live in a way that fits the calling you have given me. Let the name of the Lord Jesus be honored in my life, and let my deepest honor be found in belonging to him. Amen.
theological_themes: believer’s honor found in union with Christ

scripture_references.connection: Paul prays that God would make believers worthy of his calling so that the name of Jesus would be glorified in them and they in him. This is the direct biblical shape of the prayer’s closing request.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase about needing to 'leave the world before I enter the church' could be misread as requiring moral improvement before joining the visible church or coming to Christ. I rendered it as a rejection of worldly loves and hypocrisy, not as a condition for grace or church participation.

The prayer’s concern with being 'religious' before professing religion uses older language in which 'religion' can mean sincere godliness. In contemporary usage it can sound like external religiosity, so I translated the idea as heart-level reality before verbal claims.
significant_interpretive_choices: I treated 'present salvation' as the believer’s present experience of the salvation already given in Christ—especially through the Holy Spirit’s comfort, joy, assurance, and sanctifying grace—rather than as a separate second blessing.
I preserved the concrete contrast between appearance before people and reality before God, because that is central to the original’s movement from praise to self-examination and integrity.
I interpreted 'dispenser as well as partaker of grace' as sharing and stewarding God’s grace toward others, not as mediating saving grace in a sacramental or clerical sense.
